procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court, as confirmed by the High Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused, including the present appellant Dinesh Sahu alias Dinnu, filed Criminal Appeal No. 1867 of 2007 before the High Court of M.P. Principal Seat at Jabalpur challenging the Trial Court's judgment. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the Trial Court's judgment and order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Dinesh Sahu alias Dinnu, being aggrieved by the High Court's judgment and order, preferred the present appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 960 of 2021) before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the concurrent conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Penal Code, 1860, was justified.

facts: The appellant was convicted by the Trial Court for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Penal Code, 1860.
The High Court confirmed the Trial Court's judgment and order of conviction.
The case before the Supreme Court involved an appeal against these concurrent findings of guilt by the two lower courts.
The prosecution's evidence included a post-mortem report from Dr. C.S. Jain (PW-17), which stated that the victim's injuries could have been caused by the weapon recovered from the appellant.
law: The standard of proof in a criminal case requires the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts unless there is a compelling reason.
application: The Supreme Court noted that both the Trial Court and the High Court had already discussed the evidence in detail and found the appellant guilty.
Upon its own review of the evidence, the Supreme Court agreed with the lower courts' assessment.
The Court held that the prosecution had successfully proven the appellant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
Finding no good reason to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact, the Court decided to uphold the conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant's concurrent conviction was justified, found no reason to interfere with the lower courts' findings, and dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution was able to prove the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt.

facts: Many of the prosecution's material witnesses turned hostile during the trial.
However, one panch witness (Pratap Singh, PW-14) supported the prosecution's case regarding the recovery of a weapon, a Khukri, from the appellant's house.
The doctor who conducted the post-mortem (Dr. C.S. Jain, PW-17) testified that the deceased's injuries were consistent with the recovered Khukri.
A Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) report confirmed that the blood group of the deceased was found on the Khukri.
Two lower courts (the Trial Court and the High Court) had already reviewed the evidence in detail and found the appellant guilty, resulting in concurrent findings of fact.
law: The evidence of witnesses cannot be totally discarded merely because they turned hostile to the prosecution's case during the trial.
The Supreme Court is generally reluctant to interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by two lower courts.
application: The Court decided not to discard all evidence, despite many witnesses turning hostile, based on the legal principle that hostile testimony is not automatically invalid.
It found the testimony of the panch witness regarding the weapon recovery to be credible.
This testimony was strongly corroborated by scientific evidence: the doctor's opinion linking the weapon to the injuries and the FSL report linking the deceased's blood to the weapon.
The Court gave significant weight to the fact that two lower courts had already examined this same evidence and found the appellant guilty.

By combining the credible witness testimony, the corroborating scientific evidence, and the concurrent findings of the lower courts, the Supreme Court determined the prosecution had met its burden of proof.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution had successfully proven the guilt of the appellant beyond a reasonable doubt, and therefore upheld the convictions of the lower courts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution was able to prove the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt.
appellant_arguments: The provided text does not detail the appellant's specific arguments on this issue, but the act of appealing the conviction implies their position was that the prosecution had failed to do so.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the prosecution had successfully proven the charges beyond a reasonable doubt.

They placed heavy reliance on the evidence of Dr. C.S. Jain (PW-17), who conducted the post-mortem and opined that the deceased's injuries could have been caused by the weapon recovered from the appellant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court, exercising its powers under Article 136 of the Constitution, will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts unless there is a good ground to do so.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution successfully proved the appellant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, as the evidence presented, including the testimony of a panch witness supporting the weapon recovery, the medical opinion linking the weapon to the injuries, and the forensic report finding the deceased's blood on the weapon, was sufficient to uphold the concurrent findings of guilt by the lower courts.
legal_tests_applied: Standard for interfering with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts
why_appellant_lost: The Court saw no good ground to interfere with the concurrent findings of facts recorded by the lower courts.

The argument that a panch witness was unreliable because he knew the deceased was rejected, with the court stating, 'Merely because the said witness knew the deceased, it cannot be said that he was an interested witness or an unreliable witness'.
The court held that the evidence of witnesses cannot be totally discarded merely because they turned hostile to the case of the prosecution during the course of the trial.
why_respondent_won: One of the panch witnesses duly supported the case of the prosecution as regards the recovery of the alleged weapon/article, Khukri, from the house of the appellant.
The doctor who carried out the post-mortem of the deceased opined that the injuries on the body of the deceased were possible with the alleged weapon, the khukri.
The FSL report established that the blood group of the deceased was present on the khukri.
The court concluded that in view of the evidence, 'the prosecution had succeeded in proving the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt.'
